english_translation: An earthenware plate holds a meal of white maize sadza and beef stewed with cabbage, accompanied by a small plastic bottle of chilli pepper sauce on the side.

dialogue.shona: Ndiro imwechete yedhaga ine chikafu chinoti sadza rechibage chichena nyama yemombe yakasangana nekabichi. Parutivi pane kabhotoro kepurasitiki kemhiripiri.
dialogue.english: A single clay plate holds white maize sadza and beef mixed with cabbage, with a small plastic bottle of chilli on the side.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Ndiro [ndiro] • imwechete [imwechete] • yedhaga [yedhaga] • ine [ine] • chikafu [thing kafu] • chinoti [thing noti] • sadza [sadza (staple maize dish)] • rechibage [rechibage]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakasangana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakasangana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('chinoti')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'chinoti' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('chichena')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'chichena'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Earthenware Plates ('Ndiro Yedhaga'), Sadza with Beef & Chilli ('Mhiripiri')
cultural_notes.content: Serving white maize sadza, beef stew ('nyama yemombe'), and cabbage on a traditional clay plate ('ndiro yedhaga') with hot peri-peri chilli sauce ('mhiripiri') on the side is a beloved celebration of authentic Zimbabwean cuisine.

active_exercises.prompt: If someone says 'Ndinonzwa nyota, ndinoda kunwa mukaka kana mvura', what are they asking for?
options: Bread and sugar because it is morning
Maize meal and cooking oil from the market
Salt and vegetables for the evening meal
Milk or water because they feel thirsty
active_exercises.correct_answer: Milk or water because they feel thirsty

active_exercises.prompt: Choose the natural English meaning of this new sentence: 'Vana vanoda kudya chingwa nemukaka mangwanani.'
options: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
We bought sugar, salt, and vegetables yesterday.
Father is cooking meat and sadza for dinner tonight.
The bread has run out so I am going to the shop.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vana' = 'The children', 'vanoda kudya' = 'want to eat', 'chingwa nemukaka' = 'bread and milk', 'mangwanani' = 'in the morning'.

active_exercises.prompt: Your friend just passed her driving test! What do you say to congratulate her in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Makorokoto!' means 'Congratulations!' and 'nekubudirira kwako' means 'on your success'.
